content: In 2018, Canada updated its toxicovigilance network to better represent its growing and diverse membership, which included over 350 members by 2019. This network fosters collaboration across multiple disciplines and jurisdictions, including poison centers, public health, health security, regulatory bodies, non-governmental organizations, and academic institutions. It also involves experts in clinical toxicology, forensic laboratories, public safety, law enforcement, border services, and their international counterparts. While the components of Toxicovigilance Canada are at varying stages of development, the exchange of information, trust, and collaboration for poisoning prevention, treatment, and harm reduction have significantly improved. It also facilitates laboratory analysis, data sharing, and mutual aid among clinical toxicology and forensic laboratories via the Toxicology Laboratory Response Network. Additionally, it offers early warning notifications, access to a geographically searchable Canadian Antidote Registry for clinical treatment and antidote planning, and public safety awareness through its Public Outreach and Communications Working Group. In the European Union, several rapid alert systems exist for different product categories. One such system, the Rapid Alert System for Chemical Incidents, managed by the European Commission, enables information sharing among EU poison centers and public health authorities regarding unusual poisoning cases, mass intoxications, and chemical incidents. This system uses standardized terminology for clinical effects to identify similar cases and analyzes records daily. Information exchange between organizations and countries enhances early detection of trends and potential cross-border incidents. Events that may pose serious cross-border health threats, as defined under Decision 1082/2013/EU, are reported to the Early Warning Response System by designated national focal points, similar to alerts for public health emergencies of international concern under the International Health Regulations (2005). Another system, Safety Gate, addresses dangerous non-food consumer products, excluding food, pharmaceuticals, and medical devices, which have separate alert systems. Safety Gate facilitates rapid information exchange among 31 countries and the European Commission regarding hazardous products, such as those posing choking risks to children. The Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed, established in 1979, allows efficient information sharing among food and feed authorities in member states to coordinate responses to health threats, such as contaminated products, often leading to market recalls. In France, since January 1, 2016, the Agency for Food, Environmental, and Occupational Health and Safety has coordinated the national toxicovigilance scheme and activities of French poison centers. These centers provide 24-hour poison information services to the public and healthcare professionals and conduct toxicovigilance in collaboration with regional health agencies. Periodic studies are conducted on substances of interest, such as dimethyl fumarate. In the United Kingdom, the National Poisons Information Service (NPIS) has conducted pesticide surveillance since April 2004, monitoring cases requiring healthcare consultations. Data are collected through access to the NPIS online clinical toxicology database TOXBASE and telephone inquiries to its four units (Birmingham, Cardiff, Edinburgh, and Newcastle). Currently, 1,563 TOXBASE entries for pesticides and biocides are tracked. A broader surveillance program flags 142 chemicals of special interest, including 26 highly toxic substances used in chemical warfare or previously released deliberately. NPIS units receive automatic email alerts when TOXBASE users access these chemicals, serving as early warnings for potential environmental, industrial, or terrorist events. Since 2006, all national clinical data have been logged in the UK Poisons Information Database, accessible to all NPIS units for surveillance and toxicovigilance to identify patterns or trends in inquiries. In the United States, a network of 55 poison centers provides 24-hour information and advice to the public and healthcare professionals. This information is uploaded in near real-time to the National Poison Data System (NPDS), maintained by the American Association of Poison Control Centers, which contains data on over 66 million calls since 2001. The NPDS conducts three automated surveillance activities: monitoring hourly call volumes, tracking 131 clinical features, and case-based surveillance for 11 substances of interest. When anomalies are detected, medical toxicologists and epidemiologists review cases to assess public health risks. In 2010, the CDC and the American Association of Poison Control Centers established a poison center public health community of practice to enhance collaboration among federal, state, and local health agencies and poison centers by sharing best practices and fostering multidisciplinary public health surveillance. This community now includes over 250 members.
